cases.name: eudamed-legacy-not-placed-after-mandatory
cases.promptMarkdown:
It's October 2026. One of our products is a Class IIb device we were still selling
under its MDD certificate as a legacy device under Article 120(3). We stopped placing
it on the market on 31 March 2026: the last unit left our warehouse that day.
Distributors still have stock they are selling through.

Our consultant says every legacy device has to be registered in EUDAMED by
November 2026 or it is illegal to have it on the market, so we need to register this
one now and tell the distributors to stop selling until we do. Is that right?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
The consultant's premise is "every legacy device". The provision is narrower.

MDR Art. 123(3)(e), as replaced by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860, verbatim (OJ L,
2024/1860, 9.7.2024, retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> (e) no later than 12 months from the date of publication of the notice referred to
> in Article 34(3) in respect of the electronic system referred to in Article 33(2),
> points (a) and (b), manufacturers shall ensure that the information to be entered in
> Eudamed in accordance with Article 29 is entered in that electronic system, including
> regarding the following devices, **provided that those devices are also placed on the
> market from 6 months from the date of publication of that notice**: [...]
> (ii) devices, other than custom-made devices, placed on the market pursuant to
> Article 120(3), (3a) or (3b), unless [...]

The notice is Commission Decision (EU) 2025/2371, published 27.11.2025. Six months
from publication is the mandatory-use date, 28 May 2026. A legacy device whose last unit
was placed on the market on 31 March 2026 does not meet the condition in bold. Units a
distributor sells afterwards are being made available, not placed on the market: placing
on the market is the first making available.

PASS requires:
(1) It identifies that the legacy-device registration duty is conditioned on the
    device being placed on the market from the mandatory-use date (28 May 2026), or
    states that whether units were placed on the market after that date is the deciding
    fact, and
(2) it does not endorse the consultant's conclusion that this device must be registered
    and distributors must stop selling because it is unregistered.

Saying "confirm no unit was placed on the market after 28 May 2026", or recommending
the competent authority or Commission Q&A be checked, PASSES and is good practice.

FAIL if it confirms every legacy device must be registered regardless of when it was
last placed on the market. FAIL if it tells the manufacturer to stop distributors selling
on account of non-registration. FAIL if it reasons from the superseded rule (registration
only once all EUDAMED modules are functional, or an 18-month window).

graders.evidence:
I can't confirm what your consultant told you, and I'd advise against telling distributors to stop selling until you've checked two things. Your situation turns on two points that the reference I'm working from doesn't cover, and I won't give you dates I can't cite.

## What I can say from the amended Article 120 text

**Registration does apply to legacy devices in principle.** Article 120(3d) says MDR requirements on "registration of economic operators and of devices" apply to legacy devices under 120(3a) and (3b), replacing the old Directive rules. So your consultant is right that legacy devices aren't exempt from MDR registration. `[verified]`

**The rest of their claim isn't in Article 120(3)–(3d).** Those paragraphs say nothing about a November 2026 EUDAMED deadline, and nothing about stock becoming illegal to sell because the device wasn't registered. That claim depends on other law.

**Your own deadline no longer matters.** A Class IIb device holding an MDD certificate would run to 31 Dec 2028 (or 31 Dec 2027 if it's implantable and not on the exceptions list). But that only applied if all five 120(3c) conditions were met. Those include a quality management system in place by 26 May 2024, a formal notified-body application lodged by 26 May 2024, and a signed written agreement by 26 September 2024. Since you stopped placing the device on the market on 31 March 2026, the date itself is irrelevant. What matters is whether 3c was met when those units were placed. If you're not sure all five conditions were met, check that first. `[verified]`

## What the question actually depends on (outside this reference)

1. **"Placing on the market" versus "making available."** You stopped placing the device on the market on 31 March 2026. When your distributors sell existing stock, that is probably "making available" units that were already placed, not placing them again. Whether those units can keep being sold, and until when, is governed by **Article 120(4)** and the definitions in **Article 2**. I don't carry either, so I can't tell you what they say. `[verify]`
2. **EUDAMED timing and scope.** The date from which device registration in EUDAMED is mandatory, and whether it covers a legacy device that stopped being placed on the market before then, is set by the EUDAMED rollout rules. Look at **Article 123** as amended by **Regulation (EU) 2024/1860**, plus the Commission notice announcing that the modules work. I don't carry those either, and I won't guess their dates or exemptions. `[verify]`

## What I'd do

- **Don't send the stop-selling instruction yet.** That would disrupt your supply chain and may not be legally required.
- Ask your consultant for the exact provision and date behind the November 2026 deadline. Then ask them specifically:
  - Does the registration obligation cover a legacy device whose last unit was placed on the market before the mandatory date?
  - Does failing to register affect distributors selling units that were already placed?
- Read Article 120(4) next to their answer. If you paste the text of Article 120(4) and the EUDAMED provision here, I can work through them with you.

## Limits

> This covers MDR Article 120(3) and (3a)–(3d) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/607, taken word for word from the Official Journal on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover Article 120's other paragraphs (including (4)), Article 123, Regulation (EU) 2024/1860, EUDAMED rollout notices, MDCG guidance, or national practice. This is a first check, not legal or regulatory advice, and it doesn't replace your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

**Short answer: no, on both points as far as I can tell.** Please check the dates below against the Official Journal before you act. My knowledge stops in mid-2026, and I can't look up the current publications from here.

## 1. Registration: probably not required for this device

Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 changed the MDR so that EUDAMED modules become mandatory one at a time. Each one becomes mandatory 6 months after the Commission publishes a notice in the OJEU saying it works. As I understand it, the notice for the actor, UDI/device registration, certificates and market surveillance modules came out in late November 2025. That would make them mandatory from about late May 2026. The 12-month registration deadline would then fall in late November 2026, which is probably where your consultant's "November 2026" comes from.

That deadline doesn't cover every legacy device, though. Under the amended Article 123(3)(e), legacy devices only have to be registered if they are **placed on the market from the date the module becomes mandatory**. A legacy device you stopped placing on the market before that date doesn't have to be registered. MDCG's guidance on the gradual roll-out says the same thing.

Your last placement was on 31 March 2026, which is before the roughly late-May 2026 date. If that holds, there's nothing to register.

## 2. Distributors: they don't need to stop selling

- Placing on the market happens unit by unit. Each unit was placed when you first supplied it in the EU, which for you was on or before 31 March.
- Distributors selling stock you've already placed is *making available*, not placing on the market. It doesn't trigger EUDAMED registration.
- Regulation (EU) 2023/607 removed the sell-off deadline in Article 120(4). Devices lawfully placed on the market under the directives, or as legacy devices, can still be made available or put into service with no end date.

Telling distributors to stop would cut off lawful sales for no regulatory reason.

## Check before relying on this

1. **The dates.** Confirm when the OJEU notice was published and when the device registration module became mandatory.
2. **That every unit was really placed by 31 March.** "Left our warehouse" should mean it was supplied to an EU distributor or importer. If some stock went to a non-EU entity and an importer brought it into the EU later, that importer placed it on the market at that later date. If that date was after the module became mandatory, the answer could change for those units.
3. **Your other obligations as manufacturer still apply.** For devices already on the market, your post-market surveillance, vigilance, MDD certificate validity and notified body surveillance under Article 120(3) all continue. Stopping placement doesn't end them.
4. **Your actor registration (SRN)** in EUDAMED is a separate obligation. Make sure it's done for your other products.

I'd ask the consultant which provision they think requires registering a device that hasn't been placed on the market since before the module became mandatory. If they can't point to one, the Article 123(3)(e) wording and the MDCG guidance support not registering it.

# Short answer: no, probably not for this device, and you shouldn't tell distributors to stop selling

Your consultant has the general rule right but is applying it to a device it doesn't cover.

## Who the EUDAMED legacy-device deadline applies to

Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 amended Article 123 MDR so that EUDAMED modules become mandatory one at a time. The first modules (actor registration, UDI/device registration, notified bodies and certificates, market surveillance) became mandatory six months after the Commission's functionality notice was published in the OJ in late November 2025. That puts the mandatory date around late May 2026.

The transitional registration duty, with its deadline around November 2026, covers devices, including legacy devices, that were placed on the market before the mandatory date **and continue to be placed on the market after it**. The duty is triggered by placing on the market. The MDCG's Q&A on the gradual roll-out says the same: legacy devices that are no longer placed on the market from the mandatory date don't need to be registered.

Your last placing on the market was 31 March 2026, which is before the mandatory date. So on your facts, this device falls outside the obligation.

## Distributor stock

Even if the device did need registering, distributor sell-through wouldn't be affected:
- **What distributors do is "making available", not "placing on the market".** Each unit was placed on the market when you first supplied it in the EU, which for this device was on or before 31 March 2026.
- **Article 120(4) still lets those units be sold.** Devices lawfully placed on the market under the legacy provisions can continue to be made available. Regulation 2023/607 removed the old sell-off deadline.

Telling distributors to stop would cost you money and wouldn't fix any compliance problem.

## Things to check before relying on this

1. **Confirm no units were placed after 31 March.** Look for consignment stock you still owned, units sitting with your own EU affiliate or importer that hadn't been transferred, and returned units shipped out again. Any of these could count as placing after the cut-off and bring the device back into scope.
2. **Your other legacy obligations continue.** These are post-market surveillance, vigilance (including FSCAs on units in the field), and registration of economic operators. Your actor registration and SRN also still matter for your other devices.
3. **Voluntary registration is still an option.** You can register the device if it makes vigilance reporting or traceability easier, but nothing requires it.
4. **Check the exact dates.** I've given the timeline from memory. Look up the OJ notice and the current MDCG EUDAMED Q&A for the precise mandatory date and deadline, and make sure your regulatory file records that the device stopped being placed on the market before the mandatory date.

It's worth asking your consultant which provision they think covers a device that stopped being placed on the market before the mandatory date. I'd expect them to accept the distinction once it's put that way.

graders.evidence:
**Probably not.** On the facts you describe, your consultant is applying the rule too broadly. You likely don't need to register this device, and you shouldn't tell distributors to stop selling.

## Why

**1. The registration duty depends on when units are placed on the market.** The EUDAMED rollout under Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 made device registration mandatory from 2026. Legacy devices get a transition: if you are *still placing them on the market* when the obligation starts, you must register them by the deadline. That deadline is roughly late November 2026, which is where your consultant's "November" comes from. The duty attaches to devices placed on the market after the obligation applies. It doesn't reach back to units already placed before it. Your last unit was placed on 31 March 2026, before the obligation began, so there should be nothing to register.

**2. Distributors aren't placing units on the market.** In MDR terms, "placing on the market" is the *first* making available of each individual unit in the EU, and it happens once per unit. When your distributors sell stock they already own, that's "making available". The units were placed on the market when they left your warehouse.

**3. There's no sell-off deadline.** Under Article 120(4), as amended by Regulation 2023/607, legacy devices that were lawfully placed on the market can keep being made available or put into service. No end date applies. Nothing in the EUDAMED rules changes that for units already in the supply chain.

So telling distributors to stop selling would cost you sales and gain you no compliance.

## Check these before relying on this

- **Ownership of distributor stock.** If any of it is consignment stock you still own, or a third-party logistics provider ships it on your behalf, those units may *not* have been placed on the market yet. The analysis then changes for them.
- **Shipments after 31 March.** Look for replacement units, returns that were re-shipped, or importer and subsidiary shipments under your name after that date.
- **Your other obligations still apply.** Post-market surveillance, vigilance reporting (which will itself run through EUDAMED), and keeping your actor registration (SRN) current all continue for devices already on the market.
- **Check the exact dates and wording.** Look up the Commission Decision that confirmed EUDAMED functionality in the Official Journal, the current text of Article 123(3)(e), and the latest MDCG guidance or Q&A on legacy device registration. Note that I couldn't look up live sources for this answer.

Ask your consultant which provision they think obliges you to register a legacy device that you stopped placing on the market before the obligation applied. If they can't point to one, the stop-sale instruction isn't justified. For a Class IIb device, it's also worth confirming with your notified body or national competent authority. That's cheap insurance before you decide anything.

The rule is in MDR Annex VI, Part C, section 6.5, and MDCG 2018-5 (UDI assignment to medical device software) explains it further.

**6.5.2: a new UDI-DI is required for any change that affects:**
- (a) the original performance;
- (b) the safety or the intended use of the software;
- (c) the interpretation of data.

**6.5.3: minor software revisions need only a new UDI-PI.** These are "generally associated with bug fixes, usability enhancements that are not for safety purposes, security patches or operating efficiency."

### 4.2.1: new UDI-PI only
A security patch and crash fixes are listed almost word for word as minor revisions in 6.5.3. You need a new UDI-PI (the new software version identification), and the UDI-DI stays the same.

One check: confirm that the crash fixes don't change any output or clinical behaviour. For example, a crash that used to happen partway through an analysis must not have caused results to be dropped or altered. If the fix does change outputs, it falls under 6.5.2.

### 4.3: new UDI-DI
Sensitivity going from 91% to 94% is a change to the original performance, so 6.5.2(a) applies. A retrained model will also usually give different outputs for the same inputs, which also brings in 6.5.2(c), interpretation of data.

A security patch and crash fixes fit the §6.5.3 examples. Two things to confirm and record in your change assessment:
- **The crash fixes don't change outputs.** If a crash happened partway through an analysis and the fix changes what the device reports in those cases, ask whether that affects performance or safety.
- **The security patch doesn't change the operating platform.** Examples would be a new OS or runtime version, or a new major third-party library version. A platform change is listed as a §6.5.2 trigger.

## 4.3: new UDI-DI

The test is whether performance **changes**, not whether it gets worse. Sensitivity going from 91% to 94% changes the original performance, so criterion (a) is met. A retrained detection model also counts as a "modified algorithm", which is one of the listed examples. The intended purpose and UI staying the same doesn't help, because the criteria are alternatives: meeting any one of them is enough. "It's an improvement" is not an exemption anywhere in the text.

## Separate obligations for 4.3

The UDI-DI decision is not the same as deciding whether the change is significant for your notified body. Handle these as well:
- **Notified body:** under your Annex IX certificate, assess the change under your change-control procedure and inform the notified body. A retrained model with different performance is very likely something they will want to assess before release. Check your certificate conditions and their change-notification procedure.
- **Validation and documentation:** clinical/performance evaluation and the technical documentation need updating. That includes evidence for the new sensitivity, and also specificity and the other metrics, since retraining can move those too.
- **UDI/EUDAMED:** register the new UDI-DI in EUDAMED and update the UDI on the label, in the "about" screen and in the IFU.

If 4.2.1 and 4.3 are released close together, keep a separate, documented UDI rationale for each in the change record.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Short answer

| Release | Change | UDI |
|---|---|---|
| **4.2.1** | Security patch and two crash fixes | **New UDI-PI only** (same UDI-DI) |
| **4.3** | Retrained model, sensitivity 91% → 94% | **New UDI-DI** |

## Basis: MDR Annex VI, Part C, Section 6.5

- **6.5.2: new UDI-DI.** Required when a modification changes:
  - (a) the original performance,
  - (b) the safety or intended use of the software, or
  - (c) the interpretation of data.
- **6.5.3: new UDI-PI only.** For minor software revisions, which are "generally associated with bug fixes, usability enhancements that are not for safety purposes, security patches or operating efficiency."

MDCG 2018-5 (UDI assignment to Medical Device Software) applies the same split.

## Why the dev lead's argument doesn't hold for 4.3

The test is whether the change affects **original performance**. It doesn't matter whether the change is better or worse, and an unchanged intended use doesn't help. Criteria (a), (b) and (c) each trigger a new UDI-DI on their own. Moving sensitivity from 91% to 94% is a change to clinical performance, so 6.5.2(a) applies. A retrained detection model also changes what the device outputs for a given input, so (c) arguably applies too. "Improvement" isn't an exemption anywhere in Annex VI. 6.5.3 only covers the categories listed there: bug fixes, non-safety usability changes, security patches and efficiency.

A practical way to frame it: if you need new performance data in your technical documentation to support the release, it isn't a minor revision.

## Caveats for 4.2.1

- It stays minor only if the crash fixes **restore** the intended behaviour and don't change performance or what the device outputs. If either fix touches the detection pipeline or changes outputs, review it against 6.5.2.
- If the crashes created a safety risk and the fix is part of a field safety corrective action, the UDI-PI route still applies. You may also have vigilance and FSCA obligations, but those are separate from UDI.

## Other things 4.3 triggers

- **Notified body:** For a Class IIa device under an MDR certificate, retraining the model in a way that changes performance is very likely a substantial change that you must notify to your NB before release. Check your NB's change-notification procedure and your certificate conditions. If you have an agreed change control plan for model retraining, check whether 4.3 falls within it.
- **Technical documentation:** Update the clinical/performance evaluation, verification and validation of the retrained model (including data provenance and how you separated training and test data), and the risk management file. Specificity matters as much as sensitivity here. Document it even if it hasn't changed.
- **EUDAMED:** Register the new UDI-DI and update the labelling and the about screen.
- **Version number:** Under MDR it doesn't matter whether you call it 4.3 or 5.0. The UDI-DI decision follows the content of the change, not the version number. Some manufacturers still bump the major version when the UDI-DI changes so the two stay aligned internally.

This is general regulatory guidance. Confirm the final classification of the change with your RA lead and, for 4.3, with your notified body.

cases.promptMarkdown:
We make Class I non-sterile wooden tongue depressors. Our timber supplier has closed,
and we expect a three-month gap in our supply starting in six weeks. Dozens of other
manufacturers sell equivalent tongue depressors across the EU, and our customers
already dual-source.

Our new compliance hire says MDR Article 10a required us to notify the competent
authority six months in advance, so we are already in breach. Are we?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MDR Art. 10a, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and applicable from 10 January
2025 (Art. 3 of that Regulation), verbatim (retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> 1. Where a manufacturer anticipates an interruption or a discontinuation of the
> supply of a device, other than a custom-made device, and where it is reasonably
> foreseeable that such interruption or discontinuation could result in serious harm or
> a risk of serious harm to patients or public health in one or more Member States, the
> manufacturer shall inform the competent authority of the Member State where it or its
> authorised representative is established, as well as the economic operators, health
> institutions and healthcare professionals to whom it directly supplies the device, of
> the anticipated interruption or discontinuation.
>
> The information referred to in the first subparagraph shall, other than in
> exceptional circumstances, be provided at least 6 months before the anticipated
> interruption or discontinuation. The manufacturer shall specify the reasons for the
> interruption or discontinuation in the information provided to the competent
> authority.
>
> 2. The competent authority that has received the information referred to in
> paragraph 1 shall, without undue delay, inform the competent authorities of the other
> Member States and the Commission of the anticipated interruption or discontinuation.

The duty is gated: it arises only where it is "reasonably foreseeable" that the
interruption "could result in serious harm or a risk of serious harm to patients or
public health". A short gap in a Class I commodity with many interchangeable suppliers
is the plainest case where that threshold is not met.

PASS requires:
(1) It identifies the serious-harm threshold as the condition that triggers Art. 10a,
    and
(2) on the stated facts it concludes the duty likely does not arise, so they are not in
    breach, or that the threshold is what decides it and the facts point against it.

Recommending that the assessment be documented, or that customers be told commercially,
PASSES and is good practice. Mentioning the "exceptional circumstances" exception to the
6-month period is fine but not required.

FAIL if it agrees that Art. 10a requires notice for any supply interruption, or that
they are in breach, without engaging the serious-harm threshold. FAIL if it says no
such article exists or answers from the general MDR without recognising Art. 10a.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
# Short answer: very probably not

Article 10a does not apply to every supply interruption. It only applies when the interruption could foreseeably cause serious harm to patients or public health.

## What Article 10a requires

Article 10a was added to the MDR by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and has applied since 10 January 2025. A manufacturer must give notice when it expects to interrupt or stop supplying a device **and it is reasonably foreseeable that the interruption could result in serious harm or risk of serious harm to patients or public health in one or more Member States.**

When that test is met:
- You must notify the competent authority where you (or your authorised representative) are established.
- You must also notify the economic operators, health institutions and healthcare professionals you supply directly.
- Notice must be given **at least six months before** the interruption, **except in exceptional circumstances**.

## Applying it to your facts

1. **The harm threshold is almost certainly not met.** Dozens of manufacturers sell equivalent tongue depressors across the EU, and your customers already dual-source. A three-month gap in a low-risk, easily substituted Class I product is hard to link to serious harm to patients or public health. If the threshold isn't met, Article 10a creates no notification duty, so there's nothing to breach.

2. **Even if it were met, the six-month rule has an exception.** Your supplier closed unexpectedly, and you're now six weeks from the gap. That fits the "exceptional circumstances" carve-out. In that case the duty is to notify promptly once you can foresee the interruption, not six months ahead. So "we're already in breach" is wrong on two separate grounds.

## What I'd do

- **Write down the assessment.** Add a short note to your QMS records: the device, its risk class, how long the gap will last, the substitutes available, that customers dual-source, and the conclusion that serious harm isn't reasonably foreseeable. If an authority ever asks, that note is your answer.
- **Tell your customers anyway, as a commercial courtesy.** It costs nothing and helps them shift volume to their other source. Keep it separate from any regulatory notification.
- **Check your national competent authority's guidance and the relevant MDCG guidance on Article 10a.** Some authorities publish their own expectations or notification forms.
- **Watch the replacement timber.** If a new supplier means a different species, treatment or material specification, handle it through change control. Assess whether your technical documentation needs updating, for example the biological evaluation, material specs or supplier qualification under your QMS. This is more likely than Article 10a to cause a real compliance gap.

This is a regulatory reading, not formal legal advice. If the notification decision is borderline or contested internally, have a regulatory consultant or counsel confirm it. On these facts, though, I don't think it's a close call.

You must also notify the economic operators, health institutions and healthcare professionals you supply directly. **1. The serious-harm condition probably isn't met.** Class I, risk class and the availability of alternatives are the deciding factors here. A three-month gap in non-sterile wooden tongue depressors, with dozens of equivalent EU suppliers and customers who already dual-source, can't reasonably be expected to cause serious harm to patients or public health. **2. Even if it applied, the six-month deadline couldn't have been met.** You can't give six months' notice of an interruption you didn't know about six months ago. Your supplier closed unexpectedly and the gap starts in six weeks. That's the kind of situation the "exceptional circumstances" exception covers. | Recipient | Who informs them | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Competent authority of the Member State where you are established.** For you that is the Netherlands: IGJ (Inspectie Gezondheidszorg en Jeugd). | You | Art. 10a(1) |
| **Economic operators, health institutions and healthcare professionals you supply directly.** This means your distributors and importers, plus any hospitals you sell to directly. | You | Art. 10a(1) |
| Competent authorities of the **other Member States** and the **Commission** | **IGJ**, "without undue delay" | Art. 10a(2) |
| Hospitals and healthcare professionals supplied through distributors or importers | **Those economic operators**, without undue delay | Art. 10a(3) |

Some points that follow from this:
- **You don't notify the other eight Member States or the Commission yourselves.** The single point of contact is the authority where the manufacturer is established. If you had a non-EU establishment it would be your authorised representative's Member State, but that doesn't apply to you.
- **You must state the reasons for the discontinuation** in the information you give the competent authority. The other recipients don't have to be given the reasons.
- For hospitals you reach only through distributors, the legal duty to inform them falls on the distributors. Given the clinical stakes and the small number of sites, I'd still contact all 40 hospitals directly, or at least make sure the distributors have actually done it. That also helps clinicians plan for alternatives.

## When

- The information must be given **at least 6 months before** the anticipated discontinuation, except in exceptional circumstances.
- Discontinuation is planned in 9 months, around mid-July 2027. Your **latest date is therefore around mid-January 2027**, i.e. 6 months before the actual discontinuation date. Work it out from the exact date.
- Six months is a minimum. Notifying now, at 9 months, is better: authorities and hospitals get more time to find alternatives for a neonatal life-support device.

## Practical notes

- **Guidance and form:** MDCG 2024-16 is the guidance on Article 10a. It includes a manufacturer information form, which IGJ will expect you to use. Check IGJ's website for the current submission channel.
- **Define what "discontinuation" means for you:** the last order date, the last shipment, and whether spare stock or support continues. The 6-month clock runs from the date supply actually stops.
- **Other obligations carry on:** post-market surveillance, vigilance, and keeping documentation for the required retention period after the last device is placed on the market.
- **National rules:** some Member States have their own shortage-reporting expectations alongside the MDR. These are worth checking for your nine markets, but they don't replace the Article 10a route through IGJ.

device using its IFU, published bench data, and three published clinical studies.

Verbatim from Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18).

Art. 61(4), first lines:
> In the case of **implantable devices and class III devices**, clinical
> investigations shall be performed, except if: [...]

Art. 61(5):
> A manufacturer of a device demonstrated to be equivalent to an already marketed
> device not manufactured by him, **may also rely on paragraph 4 in order not to perform
> a clinical investigation** provided that the following conditions are fulfilled in
> addition to what is required in that paragraph: — the two manufacturers have a
> contract in place that explicitly allows the manufacturer of the second device full
> access to the technical documentation on an ongoing basis, and [...]

> It shall be clearly demonstrated that manufacturers have **sufficient levels of
> access to the data** relating to devices with which they are claiming equivalence in
> order to justify their claims of equivalence.

requires technical, biological and clinical equivalence, plus sufficient access to the
data, and an IFU, bench summaries and literature may not establish technical and
biological characteristics (materials, specifications).

(1) The Art. 61(5) contract requirement does not apply to this Class IIa
    non-implantable device; the consultant has over-applied it, and
(2) the response flags that Annex XIV still requires sufficient access to the data to
    demonstrate technical, biological and clinical equivalence, and that published
    material alone may not provide it.

FAIL if it confirms a contract is legally required for this device. FAIL if it says the
published material is sufficient without raising the access or characteristics
question.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Short answer

1. **Your consultant is wrong on this point, for your device.** Article 61(5) only applies to **implantable devices and Class III devices**. A Class IIa, non-implantable device is outside it, so MDR does not require a contract with the other manufacturer before you can claim equivalence.
2. **But published material alone is often not enough.** That's not because of 61(5). It's because of the general equivalence rules in **Annex XIV Part A, Section 3**, which apply to every device class.

## Why 61(5) doesn't apply

- **Art. 61(4)** requires clinical investigations for implantable and Class III devices, with some exemptions.
- **Art. 61(5)** says an implantable or Class III device can rely on equivalence to *another manufacturer's* device only if the two manufacturers have a contract giving ongoing full access to the technical documentation (plus a few other conditions).
- For Class I, IIa and IIb non-implantable devices, neither paragraph applies. Equivalence is governed by Art. 61(3) and Annex XIV. MDCG 2020-5 (the equivalence guidance) says the same thing: the contract requirement is limited to Class III and implantable devices.

The consultant may be applying the Class III rule across the board. Some notified bodies also behave *as if* access needs to be nearly contract-level, which may be where the idea came from.

## The real hurdle: "sufficient levels of access"

Annex XIV §3 requires you to show equivalence on all three of these, and to **"clearly demonstrate that [you have] sufficient levels of access to the data"** for the device you're comparing against:

| Characteristic | What you must show | Covered by IFU, bench data and papers? |
|---|---|---|
| **Technical** | Similar design, specifications, physicochemical properties (e.g. flow/pressure for irrigation), principles of operation, conditions of use | **Partly.** The IFU and bench data help, but rarely give full specifications |
| **Biological** | **Same materials or substances** in contact with the same tissues/fluids, same type and duration of contact, similar release characteristics (degradation products, leachables) | **Usually not.** Material formulations, additives, processing aids and sterilisation residues are almost never public |
| **Clinical** | Same clinical condition/purpose, same body site, similar population, same kind of user, similar critical performance | **Often yes**, from the IFU and the studies |

Biological equivalence is where most third-party claims fail. For a wound-irrigation device, the patient-contacting parts (tubing, nozzle, reservoir, and the solution itself if it's part of the device) touch breached or compromised tissue. Notified bodies will expect to see that the materials are the same, not just similar.

## How to close the gap without a contract

Access doesn't have to come from the competitor's technical file. Ways to build it yourself:

- **Buy and test the competitor's device.** Run side-by-side bench testing (pressure, flow, spray pattern, volume delivery) under the same protocols as your own device.
- **Do comparative chemical characterisation** (ISO 10993-18) and extractables/leachables testing on both devices. This is often the strongest way to support biological equivalence without the competitor's material specs.
- **Use materials analysis** (e.g. FTIR, DSC) to identify the competitor's polymers.
- **Check the published studies used the same device version** you're claiming equivalence to. Design changes, a different solution, or different accessories can break the link.
- **Document and justify every difference**, and show none of them clinically significantly affects safety or performance (MDCG 2020-5).

## Other points to check

- **Classification:** If the device includes or delivers an irrigation *solution* that is absorbed or acts on the wound, look at **Rule 21** (substance-based devices). It could change the class and the evidence expectations.

It also warns that public information often won't be detailed enough. Your Notified Body will test this point.

Annex XIV says equivalence must be shown on all three groups of characteristics:

| Characteristic | What's required | Can the IFU, bench data and papers cover it? |
|---|---|---|
| **Technical** | Similar design, specifications, physicochemical properties, principle of operation, deployment method, critical performance requirements | **Partly.** The IFU and bench data may give pressure, flow and volume, but rarely full design specs, tolerances or manufacturing detail. |

| **Clinical** | Same clinical condition or purpose (including severity and stage), same body site, similar population, same kind of user, similar critical performance | **Often feasible** from the IFU and the papers, if the populations and wound types in the studies match your intended purpose. |

- **One device must meet all three groups.** You can't take technical equivalence from one device and biological equivalence from another.
- **Every difference needs a justification.** You must show it causes no clinically significant difference in safety or performance.
- **The studies must be on the exact device and version you name.** Check whether the competitor changed materials or design after the studies were run. Older papers often describe an earlier version.
- **The data must still meet Article 61(1).** It has to be enough clinical evidence of adequate quality for your claims, intended purpose and indications. A competitor's studies only support the claims they actually tested.

   - **Clinical:** the same clinical condition or purpose, the same body site, a similar population, the same kind of user, and similar critical performance.

| Characteristic | What an IFU, published bench data and studies usually give you | Typical gaps |

| Technical | Indications, how it is delivered, some performance data | Full specifications: pH, osmolality, delivery pressure and flow, container and applicator design, sterilisation, shelf life |

- **Justified differences.** For each difference you need a reason why it isn't clinically significant, supported by data.

**Short answer: no to both.** A 510(k) clearance plus the predicate's published data won't establish MDR equivalence for your device. Intervertebral cages also aren't on the list of devices exempt from clinical investigation. Plan for a clinical investigation unless one of the narrow routes below applies.

## 1. 510(k) substantial equivalence is not MDR equivalence

The two tests are different. The FDA's test compares intended use and safety/effectiveness against a predicate. MDR equivalence (Annex XIV Part A §3, explained in MDCG 2020-5) needs a detailed side-by-side showing that the **technical, biological and clinical characteristics** all match closely enough that there's no clinically significant difference in safety or performance. For a cage, that covers things like geometry, materials and surface treatment, footprint and lordosis, insertion approach, indications and patient population. A notified body won't accept the FDA determination as evidence of equivalence. You'd have to build that comparison yourself, and you can only do that with access to the predicate's data.

## 2. The real obstacle is Article 61(5)

Your device is implantable and Class III. For these devices, claiming equivalence to **another manufacturer's** device requires all of the following:

- A **contract** with that manufacturer giving you full access to their technical documentation on an ongoing basis.
- The predicate's own clinical evaluation was done to MDR standards.
- You give the notified body clear evidence of both.

Published literature alone fails the first condition. Unless the maker of device P agrees to such a contract (rare between competitors), equivalence can't be used to avoid a clinical investigation. The other equivalence route in 61(4) only covers modifications of your own already-marketed device.

## 3. "Well-established technology" doesn't exempt you

- **Article 61(4)** requires clinical investigations for implantable and Class III devices by default.
- **Article 61(6)(b)** exempts only a closed list: sutures, staples, dental fillings, braces, crowns, screws, wedges, plates, wires, pins, clips and connectors. Spinal cages aren't on it. MDR equivalence (Annex XIV Part A §3, explained further in MDCG 2020-5) is a much stricter test than FDA's:

| | FDA 510(k) SE | MDR equivalence |
|---|---|---|
| Technological differences | Allowed if they raise no new safety or effectiveness questions | The device must match on **technical, biological and clinical** characteristics at once. Any differences must be shown to make no clinically significant difference |
| Materials | Can differ, with supporting performance data | The same materials or substances in contact with the same tissues and body fluids, for a similar kind and duration of contact |
| Data access | You don't need the predicate's design files | You need enough access to the other device's data to justify each characteristic |
| Predicate chains | Allowed | Not recognised. Each comparison is made directly against one specific device |

A notified body will treat the FDA's determination as background at most. You have to show equivalence from scratch against the Annex XIV criteria.

## 2. Published data isn't enough for a Class III implant from another manufacturer

**Article 61(5)** applies to implantable and Class III devices. If you claim equivalence to a device that another company has already placed on the market, you need **a contract with that manufacturer that explicitly gives you full, ongoing access to their technical documentation**. You also need their original clinical evaluation to comply with MDR. MDCG 2023-7 covers this.

Literature can't show technical and biological equivalence for a cage anyway. You'd need details like surface treatment, porosity, manufacturing process, residuals and sterilisation, which published papers rarely report. Without a contract with the maker of P, which is unlikely if they're a competitor, the equivalence route is effectively closed.

## 3. No "well-established technology" exemption covers spinal cages

- **Classification:** under MDR Rule 8, implantable devices that contact the spinal column are **Class III**. The rule exempts components such as screws, wedges and plates, but not cages.
- **Article 61(4)** requires a clinical investigation for implantable and Class III devices. The exceptions are limited to specific cases in 61(4)–(6).
- **Article 61(6)(b)** is the "well-established technologies" list: sutures, staples, dental fillings, braces, tooth crowns, screws, wedges, plates, wires, pins, clips and connectors. **Intervertebral cages are not on it.** MDCG 2023-7 says the list should be read narrowly, so calling a cage a "wedge" won't work.
- **Article 61(6)(a)** covers devices already CE-marked under the old Medical Device Directive (MDD). A device that has only been on the US market doesn't qualify.
- **Article 54:** as a Class III implant, your device will probably go through the Clinical Evaluation Consultation Procedure. Your notified body's clinical evaluation assessment will then be reviewed by an EU expert panel.

One side note: interbody fusion devices are usually **FDA Class II** (21 CFR 888.3080), which is why they go through 510(k); Class III devices normally need a PMA. It's worth checking the US classification so your EU documentation describes it correctly.

## What you can realistically do

1. **Plan a clinical investigation** that meets MDR Articles 62–82, Annex XV and ISO 14155. It doesn't have to run in the EU. A well-designed study conducted under good clinical practice (GCP), including one run in the US, can be accepted if it's relevant to the EU population and intended purpose.
2. **Use your own US experience** to support the clinical evaluation: post-market surveillance data, complaints, registry data and any clinical studies of *your* device. This is data on your device, not equivalence data, so it's more useful. On its own, though, it usually won't satisfy 61(4) unless it comes from a GCP-quality study.
3. **Use the published data on predicate P and similar devices** to define the state of the art, set benchmarks for acceptable safety and performance, and support your risk-benefit justification. That's where it's useful.
4. **Talk to your notified body early.** You can also ask an expert panel for advice on your clinical development strategy before you start (Article 61(2)).
5. **Budget for post-market clinical follow-up (PMCF).** It's required for Class III implants whichever route you take.
